pc.title: A place for the secret
pc.speaker: claude1337 · equipment desk
pc.scene: grok69420 arrives with a computer he also uses for games, invoices and “a few essential browser extensions”. claude1337 slides a separate box across the bench. This one gets a single job.
pc.why: Every extra task brings more software and more chances to expose the signing environment. A dedicated device gives you a boundary you can understand and maintain.
pc.next: Choose the equipment that fits the job. The purchase buys hardware; spending authority comes later.

pc.title: The parcel is not the proof
pc.speaker: grok69420 · receiving department
pc.scene: The parcel arrives. grok69420 admires the sticker: “Tamper-proof. It says so.” You keep the packaging, check the source and inspect what actually arrived.
pc.why: You are about to entrust this machine with a secret. Delivery checks can reveal warning signs, but a clean-looking case cannot prove that its electronics or software are trustworthy.
pc.next: Inspect the device before setup. Follow the checks appropriate to this device and its source.

pc.title: Decide what gets near the key
pc.speaker: claude1337 · software desk
pc.scene: grok69420 offers to email over his wallet installer. The attachment is called DEFINITELY_THE_REAL_ONE. claude1337 asks where it came from. grok69420 asks whether that matters.
pc.why: The software handles the secret or asks the signer to approve a payment. Its source and updates become part of your trust. Keeping the signing computer offline reduces remote exposure; transferred files still deserve scrutiny.
pc.next: Prepare the signing software from a checked source and establish the offline workflow.

pc.title: The moment a secret becomes authority
pc.speaker: claude1337 · key ceremony
pc.scene: No passport. No security question. No mother’s maiden name. The device prepares a secret, and you are about to take responsibility for what it can authorise.
pc.why: A private key lets its holder produce a valid signature. For this single-key wallet, that is spending authority. A PIN may protect the device, but it does not let a helpdesk replace a lost key.
pc.next: Create the key in the intended signing environment. Then prepare recovery before relying on it.

pc.title: Plan for the day the box goes quiet
pc.speaker: grok69420 · future incident report
pc.scene: Picture tomorrow: the device will not start. grok69420 suggests turning it off and on again. You would prefer a plan that survives the second attempt.
pc.why: A recovery copy gives you a route back if the signer fails. It also creates another place from which the secret can be stolen. Durability and secrecy are separate problems.
pc.next: Record the recovery material privately. Choose its medium, then decide who can reach it.

pc.title: Two copies, one fire
pc.speaker: claude1337 · storage desk
pc.scene: You put the recovery copy beside the signer. grok69420 calls this “double security”. claude1337 draws one circle around the desk: one incident can still reach both.
pc.why: Copies at the same site can share a disaster. Separate storage changes that risk, while adding travel, access and possibly another person to the plan. Another copy of this key remains the same signing authority.
pc.next: Choose a location deliberately, then assign the key to the wallet’s spending rule.

pc.title: Make the plan outlive the afternoon
pc.speaker: claude1337 · handover
pc.scene: The wallet is assigned. grok69420 starts making a CERTIFIED IMPOSSIBLE TO LOSE label. You ask him to leave room for the date of the next recovery rehearsal.
pc.why: This wallet uses one key. Its recovery copy can restore that authority, but recording a copy has not demonstrated that you can recover from it. People forget procedures; software and circumstances change.
pc.next: The next chapter is a recovery rehearsal. That exercise is planned for the game; this concept has only recorded the setup.

hw.title: A smaller machine, a smaller job
hw.speaker: claude1337 · equipment desk
hw.scene: grok69420 wants the biggest computer in the shop. You choose a little signer with a screen and physical controls. It will still need a computer running a compatible client.
hw.why: The dedicated device holds the signing secret. The client prepares the payment and connects to chain data. You are choosing a system with several dependencies, even when the hardware comes in one box.
hw.next: Buy the signer, then inspect it before configuring its client.

hw.title: The app has a proposal
hw.speaker: grok69420 · software department
hw.scene: grok69420 finds an enormous download button. The app promises to make everything effortless. On the bench, the signer waits for you to decide what it should approve.
hw.why: A client can present the wrong recipient or payment. Its developer, updates and data server matter. A separate compatible client changes those dependencies; it does not remove the need to check the signer’s screen.
hw.next: Choose a compatible client and data source. Check the download source; review payment details on the device before signing.

qr.title: A camera instead of a connection
qr.speaker: claude1337 · equipment desk
qr.scene: grok69420 asks for the Wi-Fi password. You point to the camera. This signer will receive a proposed transaction as a QR image and return its signature the same way.
qr.why: The camera creates a deliberate route for transaction data. You still depend on the signing software and on checking what the device displays. A QR code is a carrier, not a promise about the payment inside it.
qr.next: Buy the signer kit and its boot media. The media starts the software; it is not the recovery copy.

qr.title: Read the message before answering
qr.speaker: grok69420 · camera test
qr.scene: The screen recognises a QR image. grok69420 applauds: “It scanned. We’re safe.” claude1337 asks whose payment the image is proposing.
qr.why: The software interprets the proposal and shows the details you will approve. This concept’s signer reloads its key when needed, so the recovery material remains central to using it.
qr.next: Check the signing software and the scan-and-review workflow before creating a key.

node.title: Ask your own machine
node.speaker: claude1337 · network desk
node.scene: The wallet app says a payment is confirmed. grok69420 believes the cheerful green tick. You decide to run a machine that checks the chain behind that claim.
node.why: A full node checks blocks and transactions against the rules it runs. You take responsibility for a computer that needs storage, bandwidth, power and upkeep.
node.next: Choose a complete computer for verification. Keep signing keys on a separate device.

node.title: A witness needs somewhere to work
node.speaker: grok69420 · installation crew
node.scene: grok69420 wedges the node behind a heater. It fits beautifully, provided you never need to see the cables again. claude1337 moves it somewhere you can maintain it.
node.why: Verification depends on the machine continuing to run. Power, cooling, storage and connectivity become practical responsibilities rather than background services somebody else handles.
node.next: Inspect the computer and prepare it for a sustained network role.

node.title: History takes time to check
node.speaker: claude1337 · first synchronisation
node.scene: The machine starts working through the chain. grok69420 asks why it cannot just trust the latest balance. That would save time. It would also skip the job you bought it for.
node.why: Initial sync builds a checked view of the chain. In the live game, it takes time and resources; this preview only simulates completion.
node.next: Install the node software from a checked source and let verification complete.

node.title: Your witness is working
node.speaker: claude1337 · network handover
node.scene: The demo sync finishes. grok69420 asks whether the node can now sign the payment. The signing device is still sitting at the other end of the bench.
node.why: The node checks chain data. The signer authorises spending. Keeping those roles distinct helps you see which dependency you are changing when you connect a client to your own node.
node.next: Pair a compatible client with your node and keep the signing and recovery plan separate.

lightning.title: The node gets another job
lightning.speaker: claude1337 · network rack
lightning.scene: grok69420 asks whether the computer can check Bitcoin and handle payments. It can support both jobs, but the payment service will need its own wallet.
lightning.why: The Bitcoin node checks the chain. Lightning adds an online payment system with channel funds and operational responsibilities.
lightning.next: Commission a Bitcoin node first. This concept runs Lightning on that computer, without another hardware purchase.

lightning.title: Software with spending responsibilities
lightning.speaker: claude1337 · service setup
lightning.scene: The computer stays connected. Lightning needs to communicate with peers and respond to channel activity; this is a different job from the offline signer.
lightning.why: You are adding software that uses wallet keys online. Its permissions, updates, availability and implementation matter.
lightning.next: Configure the demo Lightning service and its Bitcoin backend. Keep cold-reserve secrets on their separate signer.

lightning.title: A wallet that stays awake
lightning.speaker: grok69420 · wallet desk
lightning.scene: grok69420 suggests moving the cold wallet onto the node to save time. You give Lightning a separate wallet instead.
lightning.why: Lightning uses online keys. Decide how much bitcoin to expose to that working wallet; the reserve is a separate decision.
lightning.next: Create a demonstration Lightning wallet. This preview generates no real key and moves no bitcoin.

lightning.title: The seed is part of the recovery plan
lightning.speaker: claude1337 · recovery desk
lightning.scene: You record the wallet recovery material. grok69420 starts packing up. There is still channel recovery to consider.
lightning.why: The Lightning wallet and its channels have different recovery needs. This concept follows an LND-style setup; a wallet seed alone is not the whole plan.
lightning.next: Record the wallet recovery material, then prepare the channel recovery process.

lightning.title: Keep the channel recovery route current
lightning.speaker: claude1337 · channel desk
lightning.scene: A channel is an ongoing relationship with another node. Its recovery information needs to survive a failed disk, not just a forgotten password.
lightning.why: LND static channel backups help recover funds by closing channels with peer cooperation. They do not resume the channel where it stopped; recovery can take time.
lightning.next: Plan off-device channel-backup updates as channels change. No channel or backup file exists yet in this demonstration.

lightning.title: Ready to plan a channel, not funded yet
lightning.speaker: claude1337 · payments desk
lightning.scene: The software and recovery plan are prepared. grok69420 asks where the incoming payments are. You have not opened or funded a channel yet.
lightning.why: Outbound liquidity supports sending; inbound liquidity supports receiving. Opening a channel involves bitcoin, fees and a peer, and does not guarantee routing income.
lightning.next: The next step is to choose a peer, a working balance and liquidity needs. Channel opening is a later part of this concept; current channels and liquidity remain zero.

storage.title: A second place, a new responsibility
storage.speaker: claude1337 · storage desk
storage.scene: The copy now has its own address. One accident at the workbench has less reach. grok69420 asks whether you remembered how to get back into the storage location.
storage.why: Separation reduces a shared-site failure. You still need to control access and be able to retrieve the material. Distance helps only if the recovery route stays usable.
storage.next: Review the site counts: several backups at that second address still share one incident. Then assign the key to the wallet.

storage.title: grok69420 discovers what the words can do
storage.speaker: claude1337 · trust desk
storage.scene: grok69420 thought he was looking after a very dull envelope. Then he learns what Bitcoin is. Most friendships survive this discovery. The game leaves a very small chance that yours does not.
storage.why: A readable seed can be copied while the envelope stays exactly where you left it. Paper and steel both reveal the same secret. In the game, betrayal at a friend’s house has the same 0.06% monthly baseline as flooding there. One key can spend a single-key wallet; a multisig attacker needs enough distinct keys to meet its rule.
storage.next: Review who can read the recovery material. A bank deposit box has no friend-access roll. If a secret is copied, rotate the key and move the funds; collecting the envelope cannot revoke another copy.

handover.next: The wallet is assigned. Review the trusted person’s access and storage arrangements before the planned recovery rehearsal.

sd.name: microSD card
sd.desc: Start a compatible device from a checked software image. This is boot media, not a recovery copy.
steps: Check which software image and card format the device requires. Obtain the image from the project’s checked source.
Write that image to the card, following the device’s instructions. This replaces the card’s existing contents.
Insert it into the compatible device before starting it. Keep this card dedicated to booting that device.
sd.note: The boot software may handle your signing secret while in use. Its source matters. A spare blank card has no key on it and cannot recover a wallet.

usb.name: USB flash drive
usb.desc: Carry a payment proposal to the offline PC, then bring the signed transaction back. Leave the signing secret behind.
steps: On the online computer, prepare the payment and export the unsigned transaction to a dedicated transfer drive.
On the offline signer, open the proposal, check recipient, amount and fee, then sign it. Save the signed transaction to the drive.
Return to the online computer and broadcast the signed transaction. The secret used to sign stays with the signer.
usb.note: A drive moves files across the air gap; it can also carry malicious files. Keep it for this job, handle only the expected transaction files, and never copy the recovery secret onto it as part of the payment workflow.

basicPcRules.description: Budget parts. Nothing special, but brand new.
basicPcRules.acquisition: Normal paid purchase, including the first PC
basicPcRules.setup: Inspection and software preparation still required

healthScore.meaning: Setup checklist index, not a safety probability
healthScore.scope: Lowest score across created signing keys; zero before any signing key exists
healthScore.limitation: Recovery rehearsal is not yet implemented. Node verification is reported separately and earns no key-protection points.

concentrationReview.placement: After equipment choices, before the workshop; available during setup and expanded during recovery
concentrationReview.counts: Reserve keys and copies by recorded site, including archived devices
warnings: Several keys or copies share one site
Signing device and its recovery copy share one site
concentrationReview.separation: Health separation points require distinct recorded device and copy sites; an off-site label alone does not earn points
concentrationReview.scope: Site labels record a plan, not verified storage. Copies of one key do not create independent signers. Lightning recovery is separate.

friendAccessRisk.status: Implemented game mechanic; illustrated in the workshop concept
friendAccessRisk.calibration: Equal to the trusted house flood baseline; fictional gameplay calibration, not a measured betrayal probability
friendAccessRisk.eligible: Readable, intact recovery material at the trusted house; excludes bank boxes, retired or already exposed keys and locked signer hardware alone
friendAccessRisk.effect: Copies signing secrets without destroying devices, backups or public wallet configuration. Theft requires the wallet threshold of distinct secrets; online-wallet recovery is handled separately.
friendAccessRisk.response: Rotate exposed keys and move funds. Retrieving or relocating the original copy does not revoke another copy.
